description: We are Bicol University CS students competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, combining full-stack dev and AI/ML to build data-driven apps. We have the technical engine covered—now we need a Graphic / UI Designer to craft stunning interfaces and pitch assets. Join us to make an impact!
summary:
MissionForge is a Godot 4 aerospace engineering simulation that turns real-world NASA flight data into an interactive spacecraft design experience. As aerospace flight directors, players build and operate custom robotic probes, orbiters, and rovers for Earth climate observation, lunar polar prospecting, and Martian astrobiology.

The platform pairs a modular 3D spacecraft designer with an aerospace multi-physics engine. Using 27 flight-heritage components across seven subsystems—structure, power, instruments, communications, propulsion, landing systems, and radiation-hardened avionics—players engineer vehicles strictly validated against real physics, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, power curves, orbital eclipse cycles, solar flux inverse-square laws, and deep-space telemetry limits.

During live flight in authentic regimes like Landsat’s 705 km Sun-synchronous orbit and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s 255 km survey path, real-time telemetry tracks delta-V, thermal stability, memory pipelines, and maneuvers. Surface missions feature autonomous Mars 2020-style descents with supersonic parachutes and Sky Crane touchdowns, followed by rover science using mast cameras, laser spectrometers, and rock-coring drills. Finally, an evaluation engine scores performance across five quantitative sub-indices, delivering root-cause diagnostics and NASA takeaways that highlight the real-world balance of mass, budget, and discovery.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

MissionForge is an interactive aerospace engineering simulation and spacecraft design platform that places players in the role of an aerospace flight director. Users design, validate, and operate custom robotic probes, orbiters, and surface rovers across three realistic mission profiles: Earth climate observation, lunar polar prospecting, and Martian astrobiology.

The platform operates through a three-phase engineering workflow:

  1. Modular 3D Spacecraft Design & Validation: Players assemble spacecraft from 27 flight-heritage components across seven core subsystems (structure, power, instruments, communications, propulsion, landing systems, and radiation-hardened avionics). Before launch, a multi-physics validation engine checks the build against real aerospace constraints—including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, power generation curves, orbital eclipse dark cycles, solar flux inverse-square laws, and deep-space telemetry bandwidth limits.
  2. Real-Time Flight & Surface Execution: Players execute maneuvers and manage live telemetry (tracking delta-V expenditure, thermal stability, and solid-state memory pipelines) in authentic orbital regimes, such as Landsat’s 705 km Sun-synchronous orbit, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s 100 km polar track, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s 255 km survey path. Surface missions feature autonomous Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) sequences modeled on NASA’s Mars 2020 mission—complete with supersonic parachutes and rocket-powered Sky Crane bridle touchdowns—followed by surface operations using mast cameras, laser spectrometers, and rock-coring drills.
  3. Post-Mission Engineering Evaluation: Upon completion, an evaluation engine analyzes flight data across five quantitative aerospace sub-indices to compute a Mission Performance Index, providing root-cause failure diagnostics and real-world NASA educational takeaways.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Bridging Theory and Practice: Textbooks often teach orbital mechanics, thermodynamics, and propulsion in isolation. MissionForge demonstrates how these systems interact in real time—showing, for example, how adding a heavier scientific instrument cascades into higher fuel requirements, tighter power margins, and stricter thermal limits.
  • Accessible STEM Education: By translating complex NASA mission architectures and flight telemetry into an intuitive visual simulation, the platform lowers the barrier to entry for students, educators, and space enthusiasts exploring systems engineering.
  • Intended Impact: MissionForge aims to inspire the next generation of aerospace engineers and mission designers by fostering systems-level thinking. Rather than treating spaceflight as trial-and-error arcade gameplay, it teaches players how real-world robotic exploration balances payload mass, financial budget, engineering risk, and scientific return.

Tools, Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Game Engine & Core Framework: Godot 4, powering the modular 3D spacecraft assembly environment, real-time orbital rendering, autonomous EDL cinematics, and UI telemetry dashboards.
  • Programming Languages: GDScript and C# (used within Godot 4 for UI state management, modular component snapping, and high-speed numerical physics calculations), alongside Python for preprocessing open NASA orbital parameters, planetary ephemeris data, and component specifications.
  • Data & Reference Sources: Open NASA flight data and mission architecture documentation (referencing Landsat, LRO, MRO, and Mars 2020 Perseverance).
  • 3D Modeling & Asset Creation: Blender for creating modular spacecraft components, planetary terrain meshes, and Sky Crane deployment animations, paired with Figma for designing mission control telemetry HUDs and diagnostic interfaces.
  • Development Hardware: Standard Windows 10/11 developer workstations equipped with dedicated GPUs for real-time 3D shader rendering and physics simulation testing.

How the Project Is Creative

  • Gamifying Systems Engineering Trade-Offs: Instead of simplifying physics to make the game easier, MissionForge turns strict engineering constraints into the core creative puzzle—challenging players to innovate within tight mass, power, and budget envelopes just like real NASA mission teams.
  • Interactive Root-Cause Diagnostics: Failure in MissionForge isn't just a "Game Over" screen. The post-mission evaluation engine acts like a virtual flight-readiness review board, tracing failures back to specific subsystem bottlenecks (e.g., brownouts during lunar polar eclipses or telemetry buffer overflows) and pairing them with historical NASA lessons.
  • Cinematic Autonomy: Combining hands-on orbital management with dramatic, physics-driven autonomous EDL sequences blends technical simulation with the emotional storytelling of deep-space exploration.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Realism vs. Playability: True aerospace engineering involves months of differential equations. We calibrated the multi-physics engine so that equations like Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation and inverse-square solar flux behave authentically while delivering instant visual feedback so players can iterate rapidly without getting bogged down in spreadsheets.
  • Subsystem Interdependency: Every component choice had to meaningfully affect multiple variables—such as mass impacting delta-V, power draw affecting thermal dissipation, and distance from Earth dictating communication bitrate.
  • Educational Clarity: Telemetry readouts, failure diagnostics, and the five-factor Mission Performance Index were designed to explain why a design succeeded or failed in clear, actionable engineering terms.
  • Performance & Accessibility: By building in Godot 4 with optimized 3D assets, we ensured the simulation runs smoothly on standard student laptops without requiring high-end workstation hardware.
